## Why is there uncertainty?

| Application | Why samples help |
|:---|:---|
| Finance | Many possible market paths |
| Engineering | Variable material and system parameters |
| Image rendering | Represent all possible light paths |
| Bayesian inference | Unknown model parameters described by a high-dimensional posterior distribution |
| Neural networks | We explore selected directions in parameter space |
| Queues | Arrival and service times vary |

::: {.key-point}
In computer experiments, sampling gives us a collection of plausible scenarios that represent variability or uncertainty
:::

## How long should a trip take?

A 5-minute walk, a 30-minute train ride, and a 12-minute taxi ride are fixed

| Uncertain input | Model |
|:---|:---|
| Train wait | $W\sim\Unif(0,20)$ |
| Taxi unavailable | $B\sim\Bern(0.8)$; ready when $B=0$ |
| Taxi wait if unavailable | $E\sim\Exp(1/10)$; mean $10$ minutes |

Assume $W$, $B$, and $E$ are independent; all times are in minutes

\begin{equation*}
Y=5+W+30+BE+12=47+W+BE
\end{equation*}

::: {.key-point}
One sample means one plausible trip through these uncertain waits
:::

---

### One trip, many possible travel times

::: {style="text-align:center;"}
![](../assets/figures/trip_times.png){fig-alt="Histogram of simulated trip times, with vertical lines at the mean and 90th percentile" width=65%}
:::

20,000 simulated trips · the mean and a high percentile answer different questions

### Means, distributions, and quantiles

Let $\vX$ represent model inputs and $Y=f(\vX)$ the quantity of interest

\begin{equation*}
\vX_0,\vX_1,\ldots
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
Y_0=f(\vX_0),\;Y_1=f(\vX_1),\ldots
\end{equation*}

::: {.sampling-targets}

| Target | Sample approximation | Trip question |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Mean, $\mu$ | $\displaystyle \widehat\mu_n=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}Y_i$ | Average travel time |
| Distribution, $F$ | $\displaystyle \widehat F_n(t)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\indic(Y_i\le t)$ | Chance of arriving within $t$ minutes |
| Quantile, $Q$ | $\displaystyle \widehat Q_n(p)=\inf\{t:\widehat F_n(t)\ge p\}$ | Time to allow for a $90\%$ chance of arriving |

:::

For a quantile, $0<p<1$ specifies the desired probability

---

### A density is also a mean

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="36%"}

\begin{align*}
\varrho(t)&=\Ex\bigl[\varrho_{Y\mid Z}(t\mid Z)\bigr]\\
&\approx\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\varrho_{Y\mid Z}(t\mid Z_i)
\end{align*}

For taxi wait $Z=BE$

\begin{gather*}
\varrho_{Y\mid Z}(t\mid z)\\
=\frac{1}{20}\indic(47+z\le t<67+z)
\end{gather*}

:::
::: {.column width="4%"}
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}

![](../assets/figures/trip_density_cmc.png){fig-alt="Histogram and conditional Monte Carlo density estimate from the same 20,000 simulated trips, showing a smoother conditional estimate with the model's jumps at 47 and 67 minutes retained" width=100%}

Same $20{,}000$ simulated trips

:::
::::

::: {.key-point}
We often use histograms for densities; conditional Monte Carlo can give a smoother estimate
:::

::: {.notes}
Given the taxi wait Z=z, Y is uniform on [47+z,67+z], so its
conditional density is (1/20) times the indicator of that interval.
The plot averages these exact conditional densities over the same 20,000
taxi waits used in the preceding trip histogram. The histogram here is
normalized as a density (per minute), rather than probability per bin.
No kernel or smoothing bandwidth is used. The density has actual jumps at
47 and 67 minutes because the taxi is immediately available with positive
probability; conditional MC retains these jumps. Density identities hold
almost everywhere, with endpoint conventions immaterial to probabilities.
See [L'Ecuyer, Puchhammer, and Ben Abdellah (2022)](https://doi.org/10.1287/ijoc.2021.1135)
for conditional Monte Carlo density estimation.
:::

## How do we want to sample?

Goal: estimate $\mu=\Ex[Y]$, $F(t)$, $Q(p)$, or $\varrho(t)$

Uniform inputs can be transformed to the model's required joint distribution

\begin{equation*}
\vU\in[0,1]^d\quad\xrightarrow{\text{probability transform}}\quad \vX
\quad\xrightarrow{\text{simulation}}\quad Y=f(\vX)
\end{equation*}

- [Target distribution]{.alert}: represent the model's probabilities and dependencies
- [Accuracy]{.alert}: reduce error for a fixed number of model evaluations
- [Flexibility]{.alert}: keep earlier evaluations when adding more samples
- [Error assessment]{.alert}: judge whether the numerical answer is accurate enough

::: {.key-point}
The model sets the target distribution\
We choose how the sample points work together
:::

---

### Different ways to place the samples

Each design has $64$ points in $[0,1]^6$ · only the first two coordinates are shown

::: {style="text-align:center;"}
![](../assets/figures/sampling_schemes_six_dimensions.png){fig-alt="First-two-coordinate projections of 64 six-dimensional samples. Top row: grid, orthogonal array, IID. Bottom row: scrambled Sobol, scrambled Halton, shifted Kronecker, shifted lattice. The grid projects onto four positions." width=96%}
:::

::: {.notes}
The six-dimensional grid has two levels in every coordinate, hence 64 full
points but only four distinct positions in the displayed projection. The
strength-two orthogonal array has all 8-by-8 level combinations in every
coordinate pair. IID has random gaps and clusters. The bottom row shows
four low discrepancy methods: scrambled Sobol', scrambled Halton, shifted Kronecker, and a
randomly shifted lattice. A two-dimensional picture alone does
not establish integration accuracy for every function. These are the generator
points before periodization; the application comparisons use baker-transformed
lattice and Kronecker points.
:::

# More Evenly Placed Samples {#more-evenly-placed-samples}

What do $n$-point, $d$-dimensional designs give us?

::: {.sampling-designs}

| Design | What we gain | What limits us |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Grid | Even spacing on a Cartesian grid | Only $n^{1/d}$ values per coordinate |
| Orthogonal array<br>strength $s$ | Balanced $s$-coordinate projections | At most $n^{1/s}$ values per coordinate |
| IID | Any $n$<br>Unbiased mean<br>Familiar error assessment | Random gaps and clusters<br>$\operatorname{RMSE}=\std(Y)/\sqrt n$ |
| Low discrepancy (LD) | [Fine coordinate resolution]{.alert}<br>[Joint placement reduces gaps]{.alert}<br>[Randomization enables error assessment]{.alert} | Moderate smoothness helps<br>Some designs [favor special $n$]{.alert} |

:::

::: {.notes}
The grid suffers the curse of dimensionality: a full Cartesian grid has
only n^(1/d) coordinate values. For an OA of strength s and positive integer
index lambda, the number of coordinate levels is (n/lambda)^(1/s), at most
n^(1/s), with equality at index one. Every cell of every s-coordinate
projection has the same count lambda; balance beyond s coordinates is not
guaranteed. The coordinate-value count refers to
the unjittered OA. In the earlier illustration, the OA has strength two
and index one, using eight levels in six dimensions. An eight-level full
grid there needs 8^6=262144 points, while the OA uses 64.
The plotted IID, scrambled Sobol', scrambled Halton,
shifted Kronecker, and shifted lattice designs each have 64 distinct values
in every coordinate; that fact alone does not establish integration accuracy.
With the correct input law and independent samples, the IID sample mean is
unbiased for an integrable output. For this unbiased mean estimator, RMSE
equals std(Y)/sqrt(n), provided Y has finite variance. Halving it needs four
times as many evaluations. Error
estimation using a sample variance and a confidence interval needs its usual
additional qualifications. No design is best for every integrand.
For the LD row, moderate mixed smoothness and low effective dimension can
make gains more pronounced; periodicity can particularly benefit lattice
rules. These are useful conditions, not universal requirements for every
LD method. Randomized points individually retain the uniform distribution;
independent replications allow estimation of the variability of their means.
The detailed rate depends on the construction and integrand.
:::

## Examples of how LD beats IID

### How long should a trip take? {#trip-mean-accuracy}

\begin{equation*}
\mu=\Ex[Y]=65\text{ minutes},\qquad
\operatorname{RMSE}_{\mathrm{IID}}=\sqrt{\frac{388}{3n}}
\end{equation*}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="68%"}
![](../assets/figures/trip_mean_rmse.png){fig-alt="Trip-mean RMSE for IID, scrambled Sobol, scrambled Halton, baker-transformed shifted lattice, and baker-transformed shifted Kronecker, with measured convergence exponents and reference rates" width=100%}
:::
::: {.column width="4%"}
:::
::: {.column width="28%"}
$64$ randomizations

Compared at $n=2^m$

Fitted $p$ in the legend

$\operatorname{RMSE}\approx Cn^{-p}$

Baker map: $u\mapsto1-|2u-1|$
:::
::::


::: {.notes}
All methods use the same two-uniform inverse-CDF representation of the trip.
The train wait is 20 U_1. The taxi wait is zero up to U_2=0.2, then
-10 log((1-U_2)/0.8). This has the same distribution as B E in the first
section. The exact mean is 65 and variance is 388/3. The exponential tail
creates a logarithmic endpoint singularity in the cube integrand, so the
smooth scrambled-net n^(-3/2), up to logarithms, rate is not automatically
applicable. The measured exponents are fitted over 4096 through 262144,
using 64 independent replications and fixed seeds; they are not theorems.
Every calculation and plot is in the companion notebook.
The lattice and Kronecker use a random shift followed by the measure-preserving baker/tent
map, 1-2 abs(u-1/2), before the model's inverse CDF. This matches the default
BAKER periodization in QMCPy's CubQMCLatticeG, although these comparisons use
fixed budgets rather than adaptive stopping.
:::

### Keister: an oscillatory Gaussian integral

\begin{equation*}
\mu=\mpi^{d/2}\Ex\bigl[\cos(\norm{\vX})\bigr],\qquad
\vX\sim\Norm(\vzero,\mI_d/2),\qquad d=6
\end{equation*}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="68%"}
![](../assets/figures/keister_mean_rmse.png){fig-alt="Six-dimensional Keister integral RMSE for IID, scrambled Sobol, scrambled Halton, baker-transformed shifted lattice, and baker-transformed shifted Kronecker, with measured convergence exponents and reference rates" width=100%}

Analytic reference

This is the standard Keister benchmark from B. D. Keister, Multidimensional

### A beam with uncertain stiffness

A beam clamped at both ends, with position $x\in[0,1]$ along its length

\begin{gather*}
(B(x,\vZ)w''(x,\vZ))''=1,
\qquad Y(\vZ)=384w(1/2,\vZ),
\qquad \mu=\Ex[Y]\\
w(0,\vZ)=w'(0,\vZ)=w(1,\vZ)=w'(1,\vZ)=0
\end{gather*}

- [Stiffness profile]{.alert}: eight cosine modes for the log stiffness, with independent Gaussian coefficients
- [Sampling dimension]{.alert}: $d=8$ coefficients determine one stiffness profile
- [Spatial integration]{.alert}: composite four-point Gauss–Legendre quadrature on eight equal cells

The normalized midpoint deflection is $Y=1$ for uniform unit stiffness

[Synthetic model and reproducible solver in the companion notebook](https://github.com/fjhickernell/StrategicSamplingColloquium/blob/main/notebooks/StrategicSampling.ipynb){.small}

::: {.notes}
The implemented field is
B(x,Z)=exp(sum_{j=1}^8 b_j(x) Z_j - (1/2) sum_{j=1}^8 b_j(x)^2),
where b_j(x)=0.45 sqrt(2) j^(-3/2) cos(pi j x)/sqrt(sum_{k=1}^8 k^(-3)).
The sampling dimension d counts the eight random coefficients; x is the
one-dimensional physical coordinate on [0,1]. The 32 spatial quadrature
nodes lie inside a single deterministic beam solve and are not random inputs.
This is the finite random-field representation implemented in log_basis and
stiffness, with independent standard normal coefficients. The Gaussian
lognormal correction makes the stiffness mean one at every x. The coefficient
0.45 is the RMS spatial standard deviation of log stiffness over [0,1].
The field is evaluated continuously from the cosine expansion. The plotted
beam solves use 32 quadrature locations, four per spatial cell; the eight
stochastic coefficients and eight quadrature cells are separate choices.
Equilibrium and compatibility reduce the clamped-beam solve to weighted
integrals of compliance and a two-by-two linear system. These quadrature
integrals, rather than piecewise-constant material values, are discretized.
:::

## Why randomize a structured design?

A random shift or scramble retains the design's coverage pattern

- Every point is [uniformly distributed]{.alert} on the unit cube
- Independent [replications]{.alert} give a way to assess sampling variability
- Continuous randomization avoids inverse-transform [infinities]{.alert} almost surely

::: {.key-point}
Randomized low discrepancy joins organized placement with uncertainty assessment
:::

::: {.notes}
With continuous uniform randomization, a finite point set avoids the unit-cube
boundary almost surely. Finite-precision implementations still need endpoint
guards before inverse transforms; the notebook explicitly handles them.
:::

## Kernel-based discrepancy

\begin{equation*}
\mu=\Ex[f(\vX)]=\Ex[g(\vU)]
=\int_{[0,1]^d}g(\vu)\,\dif\vu
\end{equation*}

The reproducing kernel $K$ defines a Hilbert space $\cf$ of integrands

\begin{equation*}
\Dsc^2(\{\vu_i\}_{i=0}^{n-1};K)=\sup_{\norm{g}_{\cf}\le1}
\left|\int_{[0,1]^d}g(\vu)\,\dif\vu
-\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}g(\vu_i)\right|^2
\end{equation*}

\begin{equation*}
|\mu(g)-\widehat\mu_n(g)|\le\norm{g}_{\cf}\,\Dsc(\{\vu_i\}_{i=0}^{n-1};K)
\end{equation*}

- The kernel encodes [smoothness and coordinate importance]{.alert}

::: {.key-point}
The bound is usually impractical for estimating the error\
Discrepancy gives a [figure of merit]{.alert} for sampling designs
:::

::: {.notes}
The displayed node collection consists of unit-cube vectors; the Hilbert
space is an RKHS with
integrable kernel and bounded integration functional. The bound applies
when g belongs to that space; the application examples are not being
asserted to satisfy every smoothness assumption used in an arbitrary kernel.
The integrand norm is generally unavailable or difficult to bound, so this
worst-case inequality is not presented as an operational error estimate.
For a chosen kernel, discrepancy instead provides a criterion for comparing
and constructing designs for the associated function class.
The near-n^(-1) statement refers to appropriate mixed-smoothness spaces and
suitably chosen designs, not arbitrary kernels or point sets. For example,
first-order Sobolev-type spaces admit near-n^(-1) worst-case convergence.
Constants can depend on the kernel, dimension and epsilon; dimension-robust
constants require additional weight conditions. See HKS26 and the research
decks' matching discrepancy bound.
Source: the MCQMC 2026 special-session discrepancy slides and HKS26.
:::

---

### Computing discrepancy from the kernel

\begin{align*}
K_0&:=\int_{[0,1]^d}\int_{[0,1]^d}K(\vu,\vv)\,\dif\vu\,\dif\vv\\
K_1(\vu)&:=\int_{[0,1]^d}K(\vu,\vv)\,\dif\vv
\end{align*}

\begin{equation*}
\Dsc^2(\{\vu_i\}_{i=0}^{n-1};K)=K_0
-\frac2n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}K_1(\vu_i)
+\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i,j=0}^{n-1}K(\vu_i,\vu_j)
\end{equation*}

- Only the [sample points and kernel]{.alert} are needed
- No expensive model evaluations
- [Product kernels]{.alert}: $\Order(dn^2)$ arithmetic work for the direct pairwise formula

::: {.notes}
The direct pairwise formula uses n^2 kernel evaluations. A product-kernel
evaluation costs O(d), giving O(d n^2) arithmetic operations. Other kernel
representations can have different dimension costs; special kernel/design
structure can permit faster computation.
:::

---

### Expected squared and RMS discrepancy

Use one common $\vDelta\sim\Unif([0,1]^d)$ and $\vu_i^{\vDelta}=(\vu_i+\vDelta)\bmod1$

\begin{gather*}
\tK(\vt):=\int_{[0,1]^d}K\bigl((\vt+\vv)\bmod1,\vv\bigr)\,\dif\vv,
\qquad \overline K:=\int_{[0,1]^d}\tK(\vt)\,\dif\vt\\[0.5em]
\ESD(\{\vu_i\}_{i=0}^{n-1};K):=\Ex_{\vDelta}\bigl[\Dsc^2(\{\vu_i^{\vDelta}\}_{i=0}^{n-1};K)\bigr]=-\overline K+\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i,j=0}^{n-1}\tK\bigl((\vu_i-\vu_j)\bmod1\bigr)
\end{gather*}

[RMS discrepancy]{.alert}: $\sqrt{\Ex[\Dsc^2]}$

| Sampling | Typical RMS discrepancy |
|:---|:---|
| IID | $\Order(n^{-1/2})$ |
| LD, modest mixed smoothness | $\Order(n^{-1+\epsilon})$ |
| Some randomized LD, greater mixed smoothness | $\Order(n^{-3/2+\epsilon})$ |

::: {.small}
Suitable kernels and designs; any $\epsilon>0$
:::

::: {.notes}
The shift formula applies to every prefix length n. The table summarizes
typical attainable rates, not guarantees for every kernel or point set.
In the general RMS definition, expectation is over the sampling method:
independent points for IID, a shift or scramble for randomized LD, and a
trivial expectation for a deterministic design. Thus the table's RMS is
not restricted to the common-shift ESD defined above.
For IID, E[D^2]=(integral K(u,u) du-K_0)/n, assuming the finite kernel
integrals needed here. The LD rates use appropriate mixed-smoothness kernels.
Some scrambled nets achieve root mean square discrepancy
O(n^(-3/2) (log n)^((d-1)/2)) for sufficiently smooth kernels at suitable
net sample sizes. For fixed dimension, logarithmic factors are absorbed
in n^epsilon; constants may depend on the kernel, dimension, and epsilon.
The faster rate is not asserted at every arbitrary prefix; the next slide
introduces favored sample sizes. These are discrepancy rates, distinct
from fixed-integrand RMSE, and do not certify the preceding application rates.
Source: [Hickernell and Yue (2001), The Mean Square Discrepancy of Scrambled
(t,s)-Sequences](https://doi.org/10.1137/S0036142999358019).

All shifts and differences are componentwise modulo one. The shift-averaged
kernel depends only on the difference of the two nodes, and its integral
bar K equals K_0 from the preceding slide. Expected squared discrepancy is
an average of squared worst-case errors; it is not identical to the variance
for one fixed integrand. For g in the RKHS, its shift-averaged squared error
is bounded by norm(g)^2 times ESD. This is the general random-shift identity
from the MCQMC 2026 special-session talk. The notebook checks the kernel-sum
identity and the random-shift formula numerically.
:::

## The catch: favored sample sizes

| Design | Natural prefixes |
|:---|:---|
| IID | Every $n$ |
| Scrambled Sobol' and base-two embedded lattices | Strongest balance at $n=2^m$ |
| Halton and Kronecker sequences | Every $n$ |

Why [not]{.alert} a favored sample size?

- Budget constraints
- Missing data $f(\vX_i)$

## Lattice prefixes between favored sizes

::: {style="text-align:center;"}

# Recent Work: Flexible Sample Sizes {#recent-work-flexible-low-discrepancy}

An [extensible sequence]{.alert} keeps every prefix

What is the [quality of every prefix]{.alert}, not just the full preferred blocks?

<h3>The best one can expect</h3>

Under the [discrepancy assumptions in Bonus material](#bonus-material)

Suppose preferred sample sizes, $n_m$, satisfy $\Dsc(\{\vu_i\}_{i=0}^{n_m-1};K)\le Cn_m^{-p}$, $m=0,1,\ldots$

- Losing or adding a [bounded number]{.alert} of arbitrary points
  - Keep the [same rate]{.alert} when $p\le1$
  - Still get $\Order(n^{-1})$ when $p>1$
- Losing or adding a [fraction $\alpha<1$]{.alert} of the points: guarantee $\Order(n_m^{-p}+\alpha)$
- $p>1$ requires [unbounded gaps]{.alert} between preferred sample sizes, $n_m$

[Proofs in Bonus material](#bonus-material){.small}

::: {.notes}
The node collections have equal weights and vector-valued nodes.
An edited node collection results from arbitrary additions or deletions,
so it need not remain a prefix of the original sequence. Assume a uniform
upper bound A on discrepancy for arbitrary finite point sets, as supplied
by a bounded kernel diagonal. If at most r points are changed, the triangle
inequality gives, for deletions,
D(retained nodes) <= (C N^(1-p) + A r)/(N-r); additions have denominator N+r.
For bounded r, this gives O(N^(-min(p,1))): the rate is preserved for p<=1,
and at least O(N^-1) remains when p>1. The fraction bound holds uniformly
for r<=alpha N with alpha bounded away from 1. It is an upper guarantee,
not a lower error floor or a claim that every missing-data pattern attains it.
The gap statement additionally assumes the usual positive point-set lower
bound a q^(-Q) <= D(Q_q), with a>0. The block triangle inequality then forces
preferred-size gaps to be unbounded when p>1 (and to tend to infinity under
these uniform bounds). Thus faster-than-1/n discrepancy cannot hold for every
prefix in these nondegenerate spaces. These are the mathematical results
checked against the other talk's 'The best we can hope for' and proofs slides.
:::

## Lattice and Kronecker: two ways to proceed

The base-two [van der Corput sequence]{.alert} $\phi(i)$ reverses the binary digits of $i$ after the binary point

\begin{equation*}
\phi(6)=\phi\bigl((110)_2\bigr)=(0.011)_2=3/8
\end{equation*}

![](../assets/figures/van_der_corput_prefix.svg){fig-alt="A one-dimensional number line labels phi at indices zero through six. The values in index order are zero, one half, one quarter, three quarters, one eighth, five eighths and three eighths. The point phi of six equals three eighths is highlighted." width=94%}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
### Lattice sequence

\begin{gather*}
\vu_i=\phi(i)\,\vzeta+\vDelta\pmod 1\\
\vzeta\in\naturals^d
\end{gather*}

Strong structure at powers of two
:::
::: {.column width="6%"}
:::
::: {.column width="47%"}
### Kronecker sequence

\begin{gather*}
\vu_i=i\,\vzeta+\vDelta\pmod 1\\
\vzeta\in[0,1)^d
\end{gather*}

Take another step by the same vector $\vzeta$

A natural prefix at every $n$
:::
:::

For the finite search range $n\le N$, use one random shift $\vDelta\sim\Unif([0,1)^d)$ per realization

::: {.notes}
The van der Corput map reverses the finite binary expansion of a nonnegative
integer and places it after the binary point: phi((a_m...a_0)_2) equals
(0.a_0...a_m)_2. Thus 6=(110)_2 maps to (0.011)_2=3/8.
The number line labels the seven points phi(0),...,phi(6) at their exact
positions: 0, 1/2, 1/4, 3/4, 1/8, 5/8, 3/8 in index order. Its spatial
order differs from index order. The highlighted point is the i=6 example;
the tick at 1 is an axis reference, not another sequence point.
The lattice generator is an integer d-vector; the Kronecker generator can be
reduced modulo one to [0,1)^d. All node, generator and shift symbols are vectors.
The displayed ordinary integer lattice vector represents a finite search
horizon N. A truly infinite extensible lattice uses generalized base-two
integer digits, as in Matiukha, Ding and Hickernell's background section.
The shift is common to every point within one realization and independent
across replications. These parameter domains alone do not guarantee a good
sequence; the later construction slides address generator selection.
The definitions and example were checked against the other talk's lattice
and Kronecker comparison; no visible cross-talk citation is needed here.
:::

## How do we choose a good sequence?

\begin{equation*}
\operatorname{WSESD}(N,d)=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\omega_n\,\ESD(\{\vu_i\}_{i=0}^{n-1};K),\qquad \omega_n=n^{1-\epsilon},\quad \epsilon>0
\end{equation*}

[WSESD]{.alert}: weighted sum of expected squared discrepancy over all prefixes

[ESD: expected squared discrepancy]{.alert}, $\ESD(\{\vu_i\}_{i=0}^{n-1};K)=\Ex_{\vDelta}[\Dsc^2(\{\vu_i^{\vDelta}\}_{i=0}^{n-1};K)]$

- [ESD cost]{.alert}: $\Order(dn)$, with fewer than $2n$ product-kernel terms
- [WSESD cost]{.alert}: $\Order(dN)$ per full generator, after precomputing sample-size weights

::: {.key-point}
Combine [all prefix qualities]{.alert} in one score to choose the generating vector
:::

::: {.notes}
Explain the objective and computational savings; retain the grouped formulas
below for specialist questions rather than deriving both during the talk.

\begin{align*}
\ESD_{\mathrm{lattice}}(n)
&=-\overline K+\frac1{n^2}\biggl[n\tK(\vzero)+\sum_{k=1}^{2^m-1}c_n(k)\,\tK(\phi(k)\vzeta\bmod1)\biggr]\\[0.5em]
\ESD_{\mathrm{Kronecker}}(n)
&=-\overline K+\frac1{n^2}\biggl[n\tK(\vzero)+2\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}(n-k)\,\tK(k\vzeta\bmod1)\biggr]
\end{align*}

$m=\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$; $c_n(k)$ counts ordered scalar differences equal to $\phi(k)$ modulo one

The shifted kernel tilde K and its integral bar K were defined on the earlier
random-shift slide. Both formulas group the n^2 ordered pairs by distinct
scalar differences. For the lattice, c_n(k) counts ordered scalar pairs
(i,j) with phi(i)-phi(j)=phi(k) modulo one, i,j<n. If 2^(r-1)<=k<2^r,
then c_n(k)=n-(n mod 2^r)+2 max((n mod 2^r)-2^(r-1),0).
These multiplicities are constant on dyadic blocks and can be filled in
O(2^m)=O(n) work. The Kronecker coefficient 2(n-k) combines the positive
and negative lags using the evenness of the shift-averaged kernel.
The arithmetic counts assume a product shifted kernel in usable closed form.
A fresh d-dimensional product costs O(d), hence O(d n) for one ESD and
O(d N) for the aggregated WSESD of a full generating vector. Reusing earlier
coordinate products gives O(n) and O(N), respectively, per trial coordinate.
The sample-size coefficients are precomputed; summing N separately computed
ESDs or searching a whole CBC candidate set is not claimed to cost O(d N).
The current objective uses omega_n=n^(1-epsilon), reserving w_{n,i} for
weights on function values in the integration estimator. In the lattice aggregate, the
dyadic-block weights are q_r=sum_{n=1}^N n^(-1-epsilon) c_n(k) for k in block r.
The Kronecker kernel coefficient for lag k is
2 sum_{n=k+1}^N (n-k) n^(-1-epsilon), computable from cumulative power sums.
The constant and zero-lag coefficients are respectively
-bar K sum_{n=1}^N n^(1-epsilon) and tilde K(0) sum_{n=1}^N n^(-epsilon).
Thus the full-vector WSESD cost is O(d N) after preparing sample-size weights;
the cached coordinate-candidate cost is O(N). This weighting supersedes the n-weighted objective in the
reference talk; its individual ESD identities remain unchanged.
The small positive epsilon in this aggregate weight need not be the same
parameter as the epsilon in the near-n^(-1+epsilon) discrepancy bound.
Fred does not want to specify their exact correspondence in this talk.
The notebook checks both grouped formulas against
all-pairs sums, including a non-power-of-two lattice prefix.
:::

## Component-by-component construction

For each coordinate $\ell=1,\ldots,d$, choose

\begin{equation*}
\zeta_\ell\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{z\in\mathcal C_\ell}
\operatorname{WSESD}(N,\ell;\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_{\ell-1},z)
\end{equation*}

- Keep the [previous coordinates fixed]{.alert}: $\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_{\ell-1}$
- Choose the [next coordinate]{.alert} $\zeta_\ell$ to minimize WSESD over its allowed candidates $\mathcal C_\ell$
- Fix that choice and proceed to coordinate $\ell+1$

For product kernels, with earlier-coordinate products cached

| Sequence | CBC construction cost |
|:---|:---|
| Lattice, $N=2^m$, fast FFT search | $\Order(dN\log N)$ |
| Kronecker, at most $M$ candidates per coordinate | $\Order(dMN)$ |

::: {.key-point .small}
For the studied kernels and suitable sample-size weights, [lattice CBC]{.alert} gives near-$n^{-1}$ root ESD for [every $1\le n\le N$]{.alert}
:::

::: {.notes}
The every-prefix theorem is for lattice CBC, not the Kronecker candidate
scan. Fix the dimension, kernel, and target rate; the constants are independent
of n and N, while the vector is chosen for each maximum N and target rate.
This does not assert one ordinary integer vector for all horizons or rates.
Source: Jiangrui manuscript 30c1f37, every-prefix corollary.

The semicolon makes the dependence of the criterion on the candidate generator
explicit. At stage ell, use the ell-dimensional criterion and hold every
previously chosen coordinate fixed. The candidate set reflects the lattice
or Kronecker construction. This is conditional minimization at each stage,
not a claim of a global minimum over all d-dimensional generating vectors.
M is the maximum size of the Kronecker candidate sets C_ell; it is not
used for another quantity in this talk. Each coordinate candidate costs
O(N) with cached previous-coordinate kernel products, giving O(d M N)
for a scan. For the lattice, fast simultaneous candidate evaluation on
a power-of-two modulus uses FFTs: O(d N log N), including the O(N)
sample-size coefficient preparation. This is the fast product-weight
CBC implementation, not a direct N-candidate scan (which would cost
O(d N^2)). Source: Jiangrui manuscript 30c1f37, fast WSESD-CBC theorem;
the construction parameter convention does not change these costs.
:::

## Low discrepancy for arbitrary $n$ {#current-prefix-comparison}

![](../assets/figures/wsesd_prefix_discrepancy.svg){fig-alt="Independent reconstruction of Jiangrui Kang's current 13-dimensional lattice benchmark. Left: root expected squared discrepancy for KCN and a WSESD lattice at every integer sample size, with the analytic IID reference. Right: one box plot of WSESD-to-KCN root ESD ratios centered between its two bounding power-of-two ticks for every open doubling interval. Each box spans the first to third quartiles, the line is the median, and whiskers show the minimum and maximum over all integer sample sizes in that interval." width=96%}

$d=13 \quad\cdot\quad 2^{10}\le n\le N=2^{20} \quad\cdot\quad \omega_n=n^{0.98}$

[94.7% of non-dyadic prefixes]{.alert} have lower root ESD than KCN

::: {.small}
Boxes: integer prefixes · whiskers: full range · below $1$ favors WSESD · worst increase $11.9\%$
:::

::: {.notes}
Current manuscript computations, independently reconstructed from the supplied
generating vectors at manuscript commit 30c1f37, November 14, 2026. This
replaces the historical 64-dimensional lattice/Kronecker plot; the new
comparison contains lattices and an analytic IID reference, no Kronecker rule.
KCN denotes the published Kuo–Cools–Nuyens embedded lattice vector
(Cools, Kuo and Nuyens, 2006, https://doi.org/10.1137/06065074X). Both lattice
vectors are fixed for maximum N=2^20 and dimension 13, with binary
radical-inverse point order. The kernel is product_j(1+j^(-2) B_2({x_j-y_j})),
where B_2(t)=t^2-t+1/6. Root ESD is invariant under a common random shift.

The displayed WSESD vector is called W_0.01 in the manuscript, whose parameter
convention uses n^(1-2 epsilon). The explicit weight n^0.98 avoids confusing
that parameter with the talk's generic n^(1-epsilon) convention. Do not state
an exact correspondence with the epsilon in the discrepancy-rate bound.

The left panel retains every integer n from 1024 through 2^20; the right
summarizes all non-dyadic n separately within each open doubling interval.
Every box is centered between its interval boundaries on the log2 n axis:
for example, the first box lies between the ticks 2^10 and 2^11. Powers of
two themselves are excluded from these boxes.
For each interval the box spans the 25th to 75th percentiles, the line is the
median, and whiskers give the full minimum-to-maximum range. There are no
random replications in this panel; the distribution is over integer n.
Ratios below
one favor WSESD. On the pooled 1,047,542 non-dyadic sizes, 992,176 improve
on KCN (94.7147%), median ratio 0.919964, worst ratio 1.119134 at n=1048568.
Pooling weights individual integers equally, so the last interval contributes
nearly half. Dyadic endpoints are not included in that percentage: 7 of 11
improve, with worst ratio 1.120865 at n=2^20. These are finite-prefix
comparisons, not a uniform superiority result or an application error estimate.

The independent reconstruction checks 48 small direct pair sums and 132
published endpoints; maximum endpoint relative difference is 5.11e-7.
All eight manuscript discrepancy win counts agree exactly. It evaluates the
supplied vectors, without certifying CBC greedy minima or rerunning the
integration experiments, whose raw arrays are stored outside the repository.
Source, command, and verification record: examples/wsesd/check_discrepancy.py
and assets/figures/wsesd_prefix_discrepancy.json.
:::

## Back to the beam: 64 lost evaluations

64 unrecoverable random losses from $2^{18}$ evaluations · first $n$ survivors

::: {style="text-align:center;"}
![](../assets/figures/beam_missing_points_rmse.png){fig-alt="Paired beam mean-error plots: the first n evaluations of the complete sequence on the left, and the first n surviving evaluations on the right. Each replication removes one uniform random set of 64 indices from the full 262144-point sample, shared across all five methods and growing prefixes. Both panels begin at n equals 64 and have trend guides with slopes minus one half and minus one. The horizontal axes count evaluations actually used." width=96%}
:::

::: {.small}
Standard QMCPy designs · $64$ randomizations · every integer $n$ used

IID: value-independent losses leave [theoretical RMSE unchanged at the same retained $n$]{.alert}
:::

::: {.key-point .small}
LD errors increase after losses, but retain a [large advantage over IID in this example]{.alert}
:::

::: {.notes}
Both panels measure empirical RMSE against an independent reference for the
mean normalized deflection of the same fixed eight-cell numerical beam model.
The reference uses 32 independent Sobol scrambles with 2^22 points each;
its mean is approximately 1.11614674373 and its replication standard error
is 2.43e-9. Three reference standard errors are 3.35% of the smallest plotted
RMSE. This is a statistical reference, not a certified continuum error bound;
spatial-discretization error is separate.
Lost evaluations are assumed unrecoverable; the estimator uses only survivors.
In each of 64 comparison replications, draw one set of 64 indices uniformly
without replacement from the full 2^18-point sample, independently of output
values. Use this same loss set across all five methods and every growing
prefix in that replication. Draw a new independent set in each replication.
The right panel averages the first n surviving values in their original order;
the left panel averages the first n complete-sequence values. Both start at
n=64. The number of losses encountered in an early prefix can be zero, one,
or more; it is not forced to be 64. The attempted prefix needed for n
survivors varies by replication and is recorded in the JSON.
Both curves show every integer n from 64 onward. The complete curve ends
at 2^18, and the survivor curve at the final available count 2^18-64=262080.
Complete and incomplete estimates use the same underlying randomized
sequence. The complete estimates reproduce the earlier beam experiment. Generators,
baker transforms, and solver resolution match the earlier application plots.
Both panels include n^(-1/2) and n^(-1) slope guides with the same
normalizations, anchored to the first complete IID and Sobol RMSE values,
respectively. These are visual trend guides, not fitted laws or guarantees.
Losses accumulate as n grows and cannot be repaired, so the slope over this
finite range need not be the asymptotic rate. Lead with the remaining LD
advantage, then explain this qualification if discussing slopes.
The full all-n RMSE arrays are saved in beam_missing_points_rmse_all_n.npz.
Per-replication checkpoint estimates, missing indices, and reference
diagnostics are in beam_missing_points_rmse.json; the notebook regenerates
the full numerical experiment.
For IID, value-independent removal leaves an IID sequence, so the two
empirical RMSE curves should be close at the same n. Finite-replication
differences remain; identical empirical curves are not required.
Fixed losses do not guarantee preservation of a rate faster than 1/n.
At the full-pool endpoint, conditional on the N output values, uniformly
removing r values adds variance r*s_N^2/[N*(N-r)] to the full mean's MSE,
where s_N^2 is the finite-sample variance with denominator N-1. Bounded
expected sample variance gives an additional RMSE term O(sqrt(r)/N).
For fixed r>=1, if that variance stays bounded away from zero, the deletion
term prevents an overall RMSE rate faster than 1/N. Value-independent
deletion preserves the IID rate at the retained count. The beam outputs need not be bounded;
this explanation uses finite second moments instead of a uniform output bound.
Within this finite-pool prefix experiment, the number of encountered losses
grows with n rather than remaining 64 in every prefix. In an attempted
prefix of length m its expected value is 64*m/2^18. Thus an apparent slope
over this range is not by itself an asymptotic-rate conclusion. Showing all
integer n also separates preferred-size troughs from typical prefix behavior.
:::

## An AI companion for QMCPy

We are developing an [AI agent to accompany QMCPy]{.alert} and assist practitioners

- Translate a practitioner's question into a sampling experiment
- Help choose designs, probability transforms, and error assessment
- Run QMCPy tools and explain the numerical evidence

[Pydantic AI]{.alert} can connect the agent to those tools

::: {.key-point}
How far can human intelligence + AI accelerate discovery?
:::

::: {.notes}
This is work in development and a direction for future research. The listed
capabilities describe the intended practitioner experience, not a released
general-purpose QMCPy assistant. Mention Pydantic AI briefly as possible
support for typed tools; omit implementation detail and the scripted demo.
The existing bounded beam prototype remains in examples/beam/ for exploration.
:::

## Take-home message

::: {.main-message}
Sample more strategically while keeping the freedom to add more as needed
:::

- LD often beats IID by [a lot]{.alert}
- Here, missing evaluations reduce LD accuracy but leave a [large advantage over IID]{.alert}
- Mathematics constructs and assesses LD sequences across sample sizes
- QMCPy makes the designs usable in simulations
- Human intelligence guides AI toward useful, checked discoveries

bound on the preferred sequence is unnecessary for these three arguments.
:::

## One identity for adding and removing points {#bonus-discrepancy-identity}

Fix the integration space $\cf$ and write $P:=\{\vu_i\}_{i=0}^{N-1}$, so $|P|=N$

Define the integration error using each collection’s own cardinality

\begin{equation*}
\operatorname{err}_P(g):=\int_{[0,1]^d}g(\vu)\,\dif\vu-\frac1{|P|}\sum_{\vu\in P}g(\vu),
\qquad \Dsc(P):=\sup_{\norm{g}_{\cf}\le1}|\operatorname{err}_P(g)|
\end{equation*}

Split the original $N$-point prefix into [retained]{.alert} points $R$ and [removed or lost]{.alert} points $L$

\begin{equation*}
P=R\sqcup L,\qquad |R|=N-r,\quad |L|=r
\end{equation*}

\begin{equation*}
N \operatorname{err}_P(g)=(N-r)\operatorname{err}_R(g)+r\operatorname{err}_L(g)
\end{equation*}

Taking norms and rearranging gives

\begin{align*}
(N-r)\Dsc(R)&\le N\Dsc(P)+r\Dsc(L)\\
r\Dsc(L)&\le N\Dsc(P)+(N-r)\Dsc(R)
\end{align*}

::: {.notes}
Treat designs as indexed point collections, so repeated locations are allowed
and sqcup partitions indices. Assume 1<=r<N; r=0 is trivial. The identity
holds for every integrand, and the inequalities follow from the norm of the
integration-error functional. The first inequality controls arbitrary
deletions. With P a longer prefix and R the preceding preferred prefix, the
second controls the intervening block for the growing-gap argument.
For additions G, the same identity reads (N+r) err_{P union G} = N err_P + r err_G.
No randomness or nesting assumption is needed for the edit inequalities.
:::

## Losing or adding a bounded number of points {#bonus-bounded-edits}

Assume $\Dsc(P)\le CN^{-p}$ and that every nonempty finite design has discrepancy at most $A$

Let $P^-$ retain any $N-r$ points, and let $P^+$ add any $r$ points

\begin{align*}
\Dsc(P^-)
&\le\frac{N\Dsc(P)+rA}{N-r}
\le\frac{CN^{1-p}+Ar}{N-r}\\[0.6em]
\Dsc(P^+)
&\le\frac{N\Dsc(P)+rA}{N+r}
\le\frac{CN^{1-p}+Ar}{N+r}
\end{align*}

For $r=\Order(1)$ and $N\to\infty$

\begin{equation*}
\Dsc(P^\pm)=\Order\bigl(N^{-\min(p,1)}\bigr)
\end{equation*}

::: {.key-point}
Keep the rate for $p\le1$; retain an $\Order(N^{-1})$ guarantee for $p>1$
:::

::: {.notes}
The edited design need not be a prefix, and removed/added points can be at
arbitrary locations. These are discrepancy upper bounds in the fixed space,
not assertions that every edited design attains the bound. A bounded kernel
diagonal supplies a finite A: if K(x,x)<=kappa^2 everywhere, the norm of
both the integration representer and every equal-weight mean representer is
at most kappa, so A=2 kappa suffices. For g in the space, multiply by its
norm to obtain an integration-error bound. Since r is bounded, N and N+-r
are asymptotically equivalent. The main talk's n uses the edited count.
:::

## Losing or adding a fraction of the points {#bonus-fraction-edits}

Under the same assumptions, let $r\le\alpha N$ with $0\le\alpha<1$

The deletion bound becomes

\begin{equation*}
\Dsc(P^-)
\le\frac{CN^{-p}+A(r/N)}{1-r/N}
\le\frac{CN^{-p}+A\alpha}{1-\alpha}
\end{equation*}

The addition bound satisfies

\begin{equation*}
\Dsc(P^+)\le CN^{-p}+A\alpha
\end{equation*}

For $\alpha\le\alpha_0<1$, both are $\Order(N^{-p}+\alpha)$

::: {.key-point}
For a fixed $\alpha>0$, the eventual upper guarantee is $\Order(\alpha)$
:::

::: {.notes}
This supplies the finite-N statement behind the main slide's O(alpha)
summary. The constant is uniform when the deleted fraction stays below a
fixed alpha_0<1; losing nearly all values introduces the displayed 1/(1-alpha)
factor. If alpha varies with N, retain both N^(-p) and alpha in the bound.
It is a worst-case upper guarantee, not a nonzero lower error floor.
The beam experiment instead chooses a fixed total of 64 random losses from
a finite pool; it does not lose a fixed positive fraction at every N.
:::

## Why faster convergence requires growing gaps {#bonus-growing-gaps}

Also assume every $q$-point design $B$ satisfies $\Dsc(B)\ge aq^{-Q}$, with $a>0$ and $Q\ge p>1$

For preferred prefixes, assume $\Dsc(\{\vu_i\}_{i=0}^{n_m-1})\le Cn_m^{-p}$

Set $q_m=n_{m+1}-n_m$ and $B_m=\{\vu_i\}_{i=n_m}^{n_{m+1}-1}$

\begin{align*}
aq_m^{-Q}
&\le\Dsc(B_m)\\
&\le\frac{C\bigl(n_{m+1}^{1-p}+n_m^{1-p}\bigr)}{q_m}
\le\frac{2C n_m^{1-p}}{q_m}
\end{align*}

Hence

\begin{equation*}
q_m\ge\left(\frac{a}{2C}\right)^{1/(Q-1)}
n_m^{(p-1)/(Q-1)}\longrightarrow\infty
\end{equation*}

::: {.key-point}
Under this lower bound, $\Order(n^{-p})$ with $p>1$ cannot hold at every prefix
:::

[Return to the flexibility claims](#recent-work-flexible-low-discrepancy){.small}

::: {.notes}
The bound uses the block inequality from the first Bonus proof, and
n_{m+1}^{1-p}<=n_m^{1-p} because p>1. The positive lower bound is an
assumption on the fixed integration space, not a property of every kernel.
Q>1 makes the exponent well defined. It is sufficient to assume a positive
minimum discrepancy for every bounded point count to conclude that the gaps
tend to infinity; the polynomial lower bound supplies this quantitative rate.
The point collection B_m denotes the intervening indexed block even if node
locations repeat. This corrects the source's incidental index notation while
preserving its argument. The constants may depend on dimension and the space.
:::
